articles.title: Ranking All 30 MLB Teams as a Free-Agent Destination For the 2026-27 Offseason
articles.summary: What are the most attractive landing spots for Major League Baseball's top free agents this winter?
articles.body:
What are the most attractive landing spots for Major League Baseball's top free agents this winter?

The two main factors in this ranking were willingness/ability to spend money and perceived contention window. Teams set up to win a World Series within the next three years and/or willing and able to make the moves necessary to improve those odds will naturally be more appealing to free agents.

Obviously, those aren't the be-all and end-all considerations for a free agent looking for the right landing spot. Things like roster fit, park factors, area of the country and countless other details could make a team more or less desirable to a particular player.

For a generic free agent looking to get paid and win a ring, though, what are the best options?

Both 2027 Cash Payroll and Five-Year Average Payroll figures per Spotrac , as of Wednesday morning.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +53000

The Rockies do have more room in their theoretical offseason budget than most, but such is life when you've suffered more than 100 losses in four consecutive seasons while doing nothing tangible to change that fate.

Coors Field is surely a more enticing destination for hitters than pitchers. In fact, it could be an ideal spot for, say, Daulton Varsho, Luis Robert Jr. or Taylor Ward to sign a one-year deal in hopes of turning a bounce-back season into a bigger contract next winter.

But if you're looking to play for a team that is likely to finish within 40 games of first place in its division every now and then, look elsewhere.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +6120

Nobody penny-pinches quite like the Miami Marlins do.

They have ranked in the bottom five in Opening Day payroll in 11 of the past 14 seasons, including three years in dead last.

After signing Giancarlo Stanton to that $325M contract in 2014, they happily allowed the Yankees to pay the vast majority of it, then traded him away the year after he won the NL MVP in 2017.

Though they've held onto Sandy Alcantara longer than expected, they still refuse to assemble a contender around him. As a result, they just completed their 22nd consecutive season with a run differential of +6 or worse—often much, much worse.

Frankly, Miami might be the best gauge of how seriously the owners believe they'll be able to institute a salary cap and floor in these CBA negotiations. If the Marlins continue to operate like the polar opposite of the Los Angeles Dodgers and don't spend in the next two weeks, it's probably a sign they aren't convinced they'll actually need to increase spending in the near future.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +10400

Though they have Bobby Witt Jr. signed through at least 2030 as part of a young core that also features Jac Caglianone and Carter Jensen, the Royals are kind of stuck between a rock and a hard place.

Payroll is already a bit high by their standards, even with Carlos Estévez, Jonathan India and Matt Strahm coming off the books. With Salvador Perez, Seth Lugo, Michael Wacha, Cole Ragans, Daniel Lynch IV, Michael Massey and Vinnie Pasquantino all slated for free agency within the next two years, there's a growing pressure to either win now or just trade away some of those pieces of the nucleus while they can still get good value from them.

That would be all well and good if they were coming off a 93-win season instead of a 93-loss season.

Both the outfield and the bullpen need a lot of work. They probably don't have room in the budget to adequately address either one.

They did, however, just trade Maikel Garcia (and two others) to Seattle for Bryce Miller (and two others). The Royals should at least have a stout rotation now, but can they score?

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +12200

Cincinnati has a quality "big three" of Elly De La Cruz, Chase Burns and 2026 NL Rookie of the Year Sal Stewart.

What else are the Reds bringing to the table in 2027, though?

Are we sure they aren't going to trade away De La Cruz, whose lack of a long-term deal is a talking point that seems to get rehashed every few weeks—even though it's pretty clear they would love to extend him if Scott Boras would allow it?

Regardless, aside from giving Burns a seven-year, $105M extension this past summer, the Reds haven't made a particularly serious investment in their roster since signing Mike Moustakas and Nick Castellanos for $64M apiece right before the pandemic hit. (Unless you want to count signing Jeimer Candelario for $45M, which was a complete disaster.)

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +11200

It should be noted that the five-year average here is a combination of a $145M payroll in 2026 with blatant tanking from 2022-24. The A's presumably do have room in their budget for a moderately sized splash or two in free agency.

This team also has a young nucleus and one of baseball's top prospects, Leo De Vries. This could be a "get in on the ground floor" type of landing spot.

Can they get back to winning on a semi-regular basis after finishing at least five consecutive seasons 10 games below .500?

How much should the combination of their current home in West Sacramento and their future home in Las Vegas factor into the decisions of free agents?

Like Coors Field, Sutter Health Park could be a nice one-year springboard for hitters hoping to rebound from a tough season. But the A's have a ton of work to do on their pitching staff before they can be taken seriously as a contender again, which raises another looming question. Who would want to make half of their starts in that launching pad in West Sacramento?

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +13700

Did you know that the San Francisco Giants have had just one winning season in the past decade?

Or that, in the past eight decades, they've had only two seasons worse than the mess they cobbled together in 2026?

Granted, injuries had a lot to do with their shortcomings this past year. Only Rafael Devers and Jung Hoo Lee made it through most of the season unscathed, and even they both ended the year on the IL. This team was all sorts of snake-bitten.

They need to add a second baseman, an outfielder, several starting pitchers and at least one high-leverage reliever before they begin to look like a team that could hang with the Padres next season, let alone the Dodgers.

The good news is that Oracle Park is enticing to free-agent pitchers, as the most home run-averse venue in the majors. With a payroll already north of $170M, it's hard to envision them rolling out the red carpet for the biggest names up for grabs—and harder to envision them reaching the postseason without a considerable infusion of talent.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +3560

Credit to the Buccos: They spent more than usual over the past calendar year, signing Ryan O'Hearn and Marcell Ozuna, trading for Brandon Lowe and extending Konnor Griffin through 2034. They even made some modest bullpen additions at the trade deadline.

It was their most legitimate attempt at mattering in quite some time. It did work to an extent, posting a rare winning record.

How much more can/will they spend, though?

Pittsburgh had a nine-figure payroll on Opening Day for the first time ever in 2026. It's already looking at a cash payroll of about $120M without having done anything yet this winter. That's also with Brandon Lowe declining the qualifying offer. If he had accepted, they would really be in uncharted waters.

Maybe they can find the room for another $10M-ish salary, but it'd be a modest stunner if they end up signing a top-25 free agent.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +6820

Every now and again, Minnesota surprises us with a big signing. Twice, the Twins signed Carlos Correa to a nine-figure contract. They also made a substantial investment in Josh Donaldson right before the world came to a halt in 2020.

Wednesday's signing of Sonny Gray to a two-year deal was also a pretty big stunner.

For the most part, though, we've spent the past few years wondering whether ownership is earnestly trying to win baseball games or whether the Pohlads are just trying to find that sweet spot of 'competent enough to entice someone to buy the franchise without putting too much more of our own money into it.'

Now, they're in a tough spot with a whole host of key players—including both the newly signed Gray and Ryan Jeffers on the one-year qualifying offer—entering either their last or next-to-last season before free agency. Their projected payroll is already north of what had been their upper limit in recent years.

They definitely need to add some bullpen arms, but we shall see how much looser the purse strings can get.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +18500

Though the Angels do have four more years left on Mike Trout's contract, they have a slightly ridiculous amount of money to spend if they're going to operate under new owner Stan Kroenke with roughly the same payroll budget they had under Arte Moreno.

Will they spend more wisely now, though, after suffering a franchise-worst 100 losses in what was their 11th consecutive losing season?

The World Series odds certainly don't paint the picture of a team that is on the cusp of turning things around. Only the Rockies are given a worse chance of winning it all in 2027.

But what if this big-market club gets busy this winter, using that copious room in the budget to bring in Teruaki Sato and a couple of arms from the "not Tarik Skubal, but could be part of a postseason rotation" tier of free agents?

Wouldn't that be enough for them to contend in a division where 81 wins were sufficient in 2026?

Being the first free agent to take the plunge would be a bit nerve-wracking, but there's some optimism percolating in Anaheim for the first time in a while.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +10100

Say this much for the Nationals: If they truly commit to winning in 2027, they could quickly become an intriguing free-agent destination.

They were already one of the highest-scoring teams in the majors in 2026. Though their payroll has been meager during an interminable rebuild, they had an Opening Day payroll north of $180M in 2018, 2019 and 2021. (They would have been north of that mark in 2020, too, had the season/pay not been truncated.)

After seven consecutive seasons finishing at least eight games below .500, can they reasonably sign enough pitching to become a contender?

Can they convince key free agents that they actually mean business now, after years of failing to lock up top players on long-term contracts?

They did at least extend both Cade Cavalli and Jacob Young in recent months, but wake us up when they decide to make a real investment for the first time since the ill-fated Stephen Strasburg re-signing.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +8900

As with the Nationals, we might be underselling the Cardinals a bit here, as they appear to be nearing the end of a multi-year rebuild and can definitely afford to spend more than they have recently.

Is this the winter that they make their pivot back to a top 10-ish payroll, though?

How are prospective free agents going to feel about the fact that it hasn't even been a full calendar year since St. Louis started dumping Sonny Gray, Willson Contreras, Nolan Arenado and Brendan Donovan in the name of getting younger and less expensive?

Some starting pitching would be great. Help at third base certainly wouldn't hurt. But there's a lot of work to be done here before anyone would reasonably expect the Cardinals to finish ahead of Milwaukee or Chicago in the NL Central next season.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +2640

For a free agent with no realistic hope of signing for an AAV of $15M or more, Cleveland could be a fantastic landing spot. At any rate, the Guardians have made the postseason in eight of the past 11 years. They haven't endured an outright awful season since the early 2010s.

Top free agents, however, rarely find their way to Cleveland, which keeps churning out postseason-caliber teams without ever spending more than it needs to.

We're about a month away from the 10-year anniversary of Edwin Encarnacion signing a three-year, $60M deal with Cleveland. That was the last time this franchise gave more than $33M to an individual free agent, as well as the last time it spent at least $55M overall in a winter of free agency.

The Guardians already have a payroll well above where they started last season ($71.7M). If anything, we expect them to trade away someone like Steven Kwan or Jo Adell rather than make a marquee addition.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +5100

You may not have felt it, but we made a sizable leap from Cleveland at No. 19 to Arizona at No. 18.

Outside of maybe Pittsburgh re-upping with Brandon Lowe or the Angels making a splash for Teruaki Sato, the bottom 12 teams on this list are not likely to sign any of the free agents destined for at least three years or at least a $19M salary.

If Jake Bauers hadn't already signed with Boston, he easily could have landed in the desert on a similar contract. If the Snakes are able to trade away Ketel Marte, they could repurpose some of those newfound funds to make a big splash for a top-10 free agent.

They've been willing to spend, most clearly self-evident in Corbin Burnes' $210M contract. Despite sharing a division with the Dodgers and Padres, they've been a solid team that keeps coming up just shy of reaching the postseason.

Maybe the next signing makes the difference.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +3800

Might as well go directly from Arizona to Texas, yeah?

Two teams who keep narrowly missing the postseason after meeting in the 2023 World Series?

Who also happens to have an aging middle infielder on a big contract (Corey Seager, in the Rangers' case) who keeps popping up in trade rumors despite possessing the ability to block any trade?

Texas has made it a point to rein in its spending a bit after paying a modest luxury tax each year from 2023-25, but they reset that clock this past season and could be a reasonable fit for either one semi-substantial contract (presumably for a starting pitcher) or a pair of smaller deals.

At any rate, it feels like a "now or never" year for them, with both Nathan Eovaldi and MacKenzie Gore one year away from free agency, while Jacob deGrom is pushing 40.

Of course, knowing a rebuilding year (or years) could be coming in 2028 may deter any free agent looking to sign for multiple years, so we'll see how Texas handles its position.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +3700

Houston has made the postseason in nine of the past 10 years, including two World Series titles.

Over the past few years, though, the Astros have just barely been hanging around the playoff picture. They're more than a little strapped for cash (and prospects) after so many consecutive years spent restocking the cupboards both in the offseason and at the trade deadline.

They need starting pitching, but we've already been speculating that it might be a "one out, one in" situation, in which they need to trade away the final year of Isaac Paredes, Jeremy Peña or Christian Walker to make it work.

Even if that's not the case and they are willing to blow right past the luxury tax threshold for a change, what's the long-term forecast here? Because in addition to those three infielders, they have one year left on both Cristian Javier and Peter Lambert, as well as two years remaining with Yordan Alvarez, Josh Hader, Hunter Brown and Yainer Diaz.

Basically, the 2029 picture in Houston looks like 39-year-old Jose Altuve, 34-year-old Carlos Correa and a mountain of unknowns.

That's not necessarily a deal-breaker, but it's something that any free agent looking to sign for more than two years would need to consider.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +3200

After three years in the gutter, the Chicago White Sox were the pleasant surprise of the 2026 campaign. They made one of the most unexpected playoff teams of all time.

In theory, now is the time for them to pounce.

After back-to-back years with one of the lowest payrolls in the sport, they ought to be spending big in free agency to ensure that 2026 doesn't become a one-off season before a return to their sub-.500 ways. To some extent, they already have, signing Dustin May to a three-year, $52.5M contract earlier this week.

Spending big has never been Chicago's M.O., though, not once signing a free agent (nor an extension) to a contract with an AAV north of $19M. (They did trade for Luis Castillo, though, who is owed $22.75M in 2027.)

We certainly expect them to pursue the likes of Freddy Peralta and Trevor Rogers. Probably Adrián Morejón, too, with reports of Grant Taylor moving into the starting rotation. Maybe they can pull it off and sign a top-10 free agent for a change.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +2320

Despite sputtering to 86 losses this past season, Seattle is a top-10 candidate for the 2027 World Series and could be a fantastic destination for a veteran seeking a ring.

How much money are the Mariners willing and able to spend, though?

Trading Luis Castillo to Chicago ahead of this past summer's deadline did shave about $13M off their 2027 ledger, but they are still looking at close to $150M in cash payroll. (For what it's worth, the Maikel Garcia / Bryce Miller trade with Kansas City basically did not change either team's payroll.)

For one of the traditional biggest spenders, $150M would imply all sorts of room for new contracts. But opening this past season with a $161.8M Opening Day payroll was already a record high for Seattle. That's why there had been speculation that the M's might be willing to trade away their final year of Logan Gilbert to create more room for spending where they need it most.

That's no longer on the table, according to president of baseball operations Jerry DiPoto, per Mariners beat writer Adam Jude . But maybe they can find the room to sign someone like Seiya Suzuki anyway.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +1910

Speaking of top 2027 contenders like Seattle, who aren't exactly renowned for their ability to bestow lavish contracts upon free agents, it's tough to say where the reigning AL champions belong in this pecking order.

Even under the new ownership of the group led by Patrick Zalupski, the Tampa Bay Rays haven't yet changed their ways. They won 98 games this past season in spite of ranking in the bottom seven in Opening Day payroll for the 16th consecutive year.

If they're still the same old Rays, it's not a question of if they'll trade away Drew Rasmussen this offseason, but rather when they'll turn what is now a one-year, $20M contract into a couple of coveted prospects.

The biggest contract Tampa Bay has ever signed in free agency was the three-year, $40M deal with Zach Eflin four winters ago. Even then, they ended up transferring more than half of that contract to Baltimore.

So, don't expect an upper-echelon free agent to sign with the Rays. But maybe do expect a one-year, $13M or two-year, $25M signing of a veteran pitcher who ends up playing a key role in this rotation. It's just what they do, as it's hard to argue with the results.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +4400

Don't mind that five-year average payroll. That's still factoring in a couple of very low-spending years in 2022 and 2023 by an Orioles team that pushed its payroll well north of $200M in 2026.

Not much to show for it this past season, of course, aside from a lot of Pete Alonso home runs in a losing season. But they're getting to hit the reset button on most of the spending that went awry, including Chris Bassitt, Zach Eflin and Andrew Kittredge.

Can they lure in some better pitchers this winter?

A short-term deal with Nick Martinez, Kevin Gausman or Robbie Ray would match their M.O. from the past few years of hoping for the best with arms that are at least 35 years old. But why couldn't Baltimore get a Freddy Peralta or a Michael King in its quest to contend in this preposterously loaded division?

They made a huge splash for the Polar Bear last winter. They just might have another up their sleeve.

One big thing that vaults the Tigers ahead of the rest of their AL Central rivals is that they've landed several upper-echelon free agents in the past.

Just last winter, they inked Framber Valdez to a three-year deal at a salary north of $38M. They're also (mercifully) on the final year of that $140M Javier Báez contract, already signed Kevin McGonigle to a $150M extension and have made a combined total of nine nine-figure signings over the past two decades.

Although they already have a projected cash payroll of roughly $170M, the budget should still allow room for at least one major acquisition this winter.

It almost certainly won't be the big acquisition. Even though the Tigers have more history with Tarik Skubal than anyone, it's pretty unlikely he'll turn down the Mets and the Dodgers to return to Detroit.

They could get one of those next-tier starting pitchers, though, or one of the several quality second basemen up for grabs.

After this, it's nothing but big-budget contenders who ended this past season with tax payrolls north of $250M.

But how could the reigning World Series champions not be a top 10 destination for free agents?

Even though it looks like their response to losing Jake Bauers to the Red Sox is backfilling with " internal candidates ," the Brewers should have room in the budget for at least one key addition.

At any rate, they've already locked up Jackson Chourio, Cooper Pratt and Luis Lara on team-friendly long-term deals. Jacob Misiorowski is still laughably cheap as a pre-arbitration superstar. Brandon Woodruff's $22M salary is no longer on the books.

There's zero chance they're signing Tarik Skubal and virtually no chance of bringing Freddy Peralta back home. Landing Sonny Gray or Clay Holmes on a two-year deal is more than feasible and could be what bumps the Brewers ahead of the Dodgers as the preseason World Series favorite.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +1570

Boston would have ranked a spot or two higher a week ago, but the recent signing of Jake Bauers may already be the full extent of noteworthy spending the Red Sox plan on doing this offseason.

Over the past few years, this franchise hasn't spent as much as it arguably should. The Red Sox were top five in Opening Day payroll every year from 2004-20, winning four World Series in the process. But they've ranked either 11th or 12th in each of the past four seasons, with an average mark of $184.5M.

So, unless they're changing their stripes, the fact that they are already well north of $200M suggests that, if anything, they'll try to shed some payroll in their remaining offseason moves.

They have the fourth-best World Series odds, though. Perhaps winning just seven postseason games over the past eight years is just the kick in the pants they needed to start investing more in winning.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +2120

Chairman and CEO of Braves Holdings, LLC, Terry McGuirk said last winter that the Atlanta Braves "aspire to be a top-five team in total payroll."

They almost got there this past season with the sixth-highest Opening Day payroll of $252M, but how much deeper can they reasonably afford to dig into those pockets?

That was about $35M higher than they had ever gone before. After their recent signing of Evan Phillips, they already have $201M in known 2027 cash payroll for their 13 highest-paid players. Even if they do nothing else, they're already looking at north of $230M once they fill out the rest of the roster with arbitration and pre-arb guys.

Yet, virtually everyone expects Atlanta to sign at least one of the top 10-ish starting pitchers available this winter. Re-signing Mauricio Dubón is plausible, if not inevitable.

Spending like either New York team, the Dodgers or the Phillies probably isn't happening. But maybe Atlanta makes enough additions to edge out the likes of Boston, Toronto and San Diego for the top-five payroll they evidently desire.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +2560

Teams under new ownership are always worth watching in free agency, as the dream scenario is to swoop in and win a World Series in the first year.

In the Padres' case, signing starting pitching is a must. Because as things presently stand, they're looking at a rotation that includes JP Sears, Jhony Brito and either Ryan Weiss or Yu Darvish, if the latter can make it back onto a big-league mound.

They do already have several very substantial contracts on the books. Manny Machado, Fernando Tatis Jr., Xander Bogaerts and Jackson Merrill are owed a combined sum of $853M over the course of the next eight years. It should be interesting to see whether José Feliciano and Kwanza Jones try to trade away any of those inherited contracts.

But San Diego will be busy this offseason, as it has been for the past half-decade.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +3400

The Blue Jays were one of the biggest disappointments of the 2026 campaign. After reaching the 2025 World Series, they signed Dylan Cease, Kazuma Okamoto and more...and suffered 15 more losses.

But buckle up for another offseason spending spree, as more than $100M in players from this 2026 Opening Day payroll are no longer on the roster.

Toronto still has a much higher payroll than most. However, the gap between its current cash payroll ($214.8M) and where it finished this past season ($305.3M) is positively massive.

That's why the Blue Jays are at least on the fringe of the Tarik Skubal conversation and have been connected to seemingly every other upper-echelon player on the market. They have both the needs and the budget to make multiple splashes.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +1920

For the umpteenth consecutive year, it feels like the Phillies are nearing the end of their championship window.

However, they are also showing no signs of taking their foot off the gas.

They have already signed a free agent to a nine-figure contract in seven of the past eight offseasons. It sure looks like they're trying to make it eight out of nine en route to yet another franchise record-setting payroll.

The Phillies are already rumored to have interest in Randy Arozarena, Seiya Suzuki and/or Teruaki Sato in their quest to address a seemingly eternal Achilles' heel in right field. Goodness knows they need to give Jhoan Duran some support in the bullpen, too, though that won't be a nine-figure investment.

2029 and 2030 could be mighty painful in Philadelphia, with Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber, Aaron Nola and Trea Turner making a combined $104M in each of their age-36 and age-37 seasons. But 2027 could be all sorts of fun in the City of Brotherly Love if and when they bring in one more big name.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +2100

The Cubs lost 17 players as free agents, including basically an entire pitching staff.

Honestly, it's hard to believe they still have a payroll north of $150M given all that they need to replace.

They will eventually be quite busy in free agency, already rumored to be interested in just about every starting pitcher under the sun.

They ended up with a cash payroll of $275M this past season and haven't been below $212M since 2022—when the Cubs were still in "quick rebuild" mode after that 2021 trade deadline fire sale that netted them Pete Crow-Armstrong. You have to think they'll be willing to add roughly $100M in 2027 salary this offseason.

Heck, they could sign Freddy Peralta, Clay Holmes, Kevin Gausman and Adrián Morejón and still not add $100M, so it should be an eventful winter in the Windy City.

2027 World Series Consensus Odds : +2480

The New York Mets are the relatively clear favorites to sign Tarik Skubal, as there remains seemingly no limit to what Steve Cohen is willing to spend to try to win.

Will they actually win for a change, though?

Through five years of gratuitous spending, the Mets have had 1.5 good seasons, winning 101 games in 2022 and then reaching the 2024 NLCS after rallying from a 24-35 start.

They've actually gone 321-327 over the past four years, despite paying a tax bill north of $90M in each of those seasons. This past season, they ended up dead last in the NL East.

The checks presumably keep coming in, though, as big free agents keep going there. They signed at least $250M worth of new contracts in four of the past five years, including north of $1 billion when they landed Juan Soto two winters ago.

Perhaps Skubal will finally be the one to get them back to the promised land?

Though they have won just one World Series in the past 26 years, the New York Yankees are still that mystical team an entire generation of baseball players dreamed of playing for (or against).

Though their spending hasn't meteorically risen in lockstep with the Mets and Dodgers, they still have a top-three payroll virtually every year, signing six free agents to contracts of at least $90M over the course of the past seven offseasons.

They also still make the playoffs far more often than not and have simply struggled to finish the fight in the postseason. So, if the goal is to make a lot of money while also playing into October, there's really only one better choice than this.

As far as what the Yankees figure to spend on this winter, it's the bullpen first and foremost. Getting David Bednar to accept the one-year qualifying offer was quite the coup, but they still have work to do. Adding a surer thing at second base would be swell, too.

Who else could it be but the new evil empire?

The Dodgers have won at least 91 games in each of the last 13 162-game seasons, and went 43-17 (116 win pace) in 2020. The only year in that stretch when they didn't win the NL West was 2021, when 106 victories left them one game shy of the Giants.

They've won three of the past seven World Series, paying handsomely for each.

Though their current tax payroll for 2027 is nearly $385M, they've deferred so much of it that their cash payroll isn't even $250M. That was the point all along with Shohei Ohtani's contract: not only signing the best player in the world, but also having the means to surround him with the best other talent that money can buy.

Maybe this will finally be the year they pump the brakes a little bit, as they don't actually need much of anything aside from maybe a middle reliever and a utility infielder.

When has it ever been about need, though? They didn't need Kyle Tucker last offseason. They still gave him $240M. So if they end up re-signing Skubal, feel free to get mad, but don't be shocked.

articles.title: Every MLB Team's Player Most Likely to Be Traded in 26-27 Offseason
articles.summary: Time is ticking until the current collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1 at 11:59 p.m. ET, after which the owners are expected to lock the players out and plunge the sport into uncertainty.
articles.body:
Time is ticking until the current collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1 at 11:59 p.m. ET, after which the owners are expected to lock the players out and plunge the sport into uncertainty.

While teams may be more active than usual in the weeks leading up to the lockout, it stands to reason that there will be quite a bit to sort out once the new CBA is in place. Among those items will be trades, a bulk of which could come when it's clearer what the future financial landscape of the sport will look like.

Regardless of when they happen, let's take a look at every MLB team's player most likely to be traded in the 2026-27 offseason.

Our initial inclination was to put Drew Rasmussen, although Ken Rosenthal, Will Sammon and Katie Woo of The Athletic reported that Tampa Bay is interested in potentially signing the two-time All-Star beyond his contract year in 2027.

We won't altogether rule out the possibility that Erik Neander and the Rays ultimately get overwhelmed for Rasmussen, who is due $20 million in 2027. But with Nick Martinez and Freddy Peralta likely to depart in free agency, the Rays probably don't want to entirely start over in the rotation after reaching the World Series.

Alternatively, the Rays "might consider" trading outfielder Jonny DeLuca, per Rosenthal and Sammon . The 28-year-old has three remaining years of arbitration eligibility and would likely draw widespread interest, considering he posted four defensive runs saved in center field this past season. Add in his .738 second-half OPS, and teams desperate for better outfield production would definitely be interested in DeLuca. The Rays, meanwhile, could slide Victor Mesa Jr. into center field full-time.

Luis Gil won the AL Rookie of the Year in 2024, going 15-7 with a 3.50 ERA across 29 starts spanning 151.2 innings. However, in the two seasons since then, Gil has been limited to just 20 appearances (16 starts).

Gil is now projected to make $3.2 million in his first year of arbitration eligibility, which would be a bargain if you could guarantee his health. History shows us you can't. He's currently slated to be on the outside looking in of Aaron Boone's rotation, which includes Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole, Carlos Rodón and Will Warren. That rotation has some age, which might make Brian Cashman inclined to hold onto rotation depth. Then again, he still has Ryan Weathers, who made 25 starts in 2026. Weathers could also be a trade candidate, as it's hard to imagine both him and Gil back in pinstripes in 2027.

Gil would be an interesting piece to roll the dice on this offseason. For example, if the Yankees become interested in Milwaukee Brewers All-Star closer Trevor Megill, Gil could be a high-upside piece for the reigning World Series Champions to get back a fan favorite for just one season.

Some wonder whether the Red Sox could end up non-tendering Jarren Duran before Friday's 5 p.m. ET deadline. That would still seem drastic, though it does feel like things have run their course for the former All-Star Game MVP in Boston.

Duran had a nightmarish 2026 season, hitting .207 with a .627 OPS in 551 at-bats for the Red Sox. He doesn't do himself any favors—even if he's being unfairly provoked— with some of his interactions with hecklers . It just seems like he needs a fresh start, perhaps in a smaller market.

Now 30, Duran has two years of arbitration eligibility left. At his best, he's a triples machine that can be the catalyst for a lineup. With Roman Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela and Wilyer Abreu, the Red Sox are set in the outfield. Plenty of other teams aren't.

Remember when an all-time great farm system had the Orioles seemingly set up to dominate the second half of the 2020s? Well, they're coming off two disappointing seasons, and some of their top prospects haven't developed as expected.

Even off a relatively underwhelming season, Gunnar Henderson would still become the most coveted player on the trade market if the Orioles made him available before his penultimate year of arbitration eligibility. The bet is that they ultimately hold on to the former AL Rookie of the Year for now.

There are still plenty of other trade possibilities to consider in Baltimore, including Jackson Holliday and Colton Cowser. Assuming they feel confident that Jordan Westburg will be healthy in 2027, though, Coby Mayo might be the one who makes the most sense. Pete Alonso is entrenched at first base. Christian Encarnacion-Strand had a big second half and showed the ability to play third. Westburg is a natural third baseman who might take the bulk of the DH at-bats to open 2027. Mayo could be a trade piece that helps the Orioles improve another area of their roster.

Set to turn 25 in December, Mayo hit 24 homers last season in 412 at-bats. He is more of a platoon player, posting a 1.105 OPS against lefties but just a .567 OPS vs. righties. That's fine; there aren't enough quality right-handed hitters in the sport today. Mayo had minus-nine defensive runs saved at third base in 2026, so he would fit best on a team with significant at-bats open at first base and/or DH.

It's kind of crazy how quickly we've arrived at this point. Clement followed up a monster postseason by leading all AL players in All-Star votes in 2026. After starting at second base in the Midsummer Classic, Clement hit just .203 in the second half.

As things stand right now, Clement is slated to be the starting second baseman for the Blue Jays in 2027. This is a loaded free-agent class at second base. General manager Ross Atkins didn't guarantee Clement will start at the position on Opening Day 2027. If the Blue Jays sign a second baseman and have Kazuma Okamoto at third base, it's hard to imagine there being enough at-bats for Clement, even with his ability to play in the outfield.

Mind you, just last October Clement set a new MLB record with 30 hits in one postseason. At a time when the sport is starved for contact hitters—particularly right-handed ones—Clement will draw significant trade interest , with two arbitration years remaining before free agency.

Steven Kwan struggled at the plate for almost a full calendar year before reemerging as one of the game's best contact hitters in the second half of 2026, batting .353 with an .879 OPS.

Add that he's won four Gold Glove Awards in left field and showed the ability to play above-average center field in 2026, Kwan figures to be coveted on the trade market this offseason.

While there may be some temptation for the Guardians to hold onto him after reaching the ALCS for the second time in three years, he'll likely be looking at a $100 million-plus contract next offseason. History tells us the Guards will trade Kwan before his walk year and somehow not skip a beat in 2027.

Joey Bart could be a non-tender candidate, as MLB Trade Rumors projects he'll make $2.9 million in his second of three arbitration years. However, teams are so desperate for a catcher that Chris Geitz and company should be able to find a taker for the former No. 2 overall pick.

Bart never developed into the franchise catcher the San Francisco Giants once thought he could be, but his .799 OPS in 2024 as a member of the Pittsburgh Pirates is going to be enough to keep teams intrigued by him as at least a part-time player.

In 2026, Bart played for three teams: the Pirates, the Atlanta Braves, and the White Sox. The three games he appeared in for the White Sox will likely be his only with the club, as they will probably move forward with some combination of Kyle Teel, Drew Romo and Edgar Quero.

Joe Ryan is going to be the trade candidate that intrigues everyone. Considering he's entering a contract year, it's hardly unreasonable to suggest his name. New control-person Tom Pohlad really seems to be trying to put his best foot forward, though, so the Twins might want to hold onto Ryan at least until the trade deadline.

Also, at this point, between his injuries and seeming unwillingness to waive his no-trade clause (although it goes from a full to a five-team one in 2027), it's fair to assume Byron Buxton is staying put.

Trevor Larnach was set to be traded to the Astros this past summer for reliever Bryan Abreu, before Houston owner Jim Crane squashed the deal, per Michael Marino . It might not be with the Astros, but if the Twins were willing to move Larnach in the summer, it's reasonable to think they will be again this winter.

Spencer Torkelson has homered 26 or more times in three separate seasons, including 2026. Yet it still feels like the former No. 1 overall pick has been a disappointment, with a .732 OPS through his first five MLB seasons. He is also coming off a career-high 194 strikeouts in 2026.

Torkelson still has three remaining years of arbitration eligibility, so the Tigers don't have to move the 27-year-old. But he feels like a change-of-scenery candidate.

President of Baseball Operations Scott Harris could make an external addition at first base, such as signing Ty France or Nathaniel Lowe. The Tigers could also view prospect José Briceño as more of a first baseman than a catcher, letting him get most of his at-bats there in 2027.

Kyle Isbel was the original selection here, but he was designated for assignment shortly before our publish time in the wake of the six-player deal that saw the Royals send Maikel Garcia to the Seattle Mariners in a trade that brought Bryce Miller back to Kansas City.

Considering the trade also brought back setup man Jose A. Ferrer, there's a strong chance the Royals won't make a more impactful move this offseason. But with the addition of Miller, perhaps Tony Gonsolin is expendable.

Gonsolin has a 5.21 ERA in parts of four seasons since he was an All-Star for the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2022. However, he's making just $2.5 million in 2027, so starter-needy clubs might be willing to roll the dice and hope he stays healthy.

Two winters ago, the Astros traded Kyle Tucker to the Chicago Cubs before his contract year because they decided they wouldn't meet his long-term asking price. A similar situation could unfold with Jeremy Peña this offseason.

Peña, 29, has an .822 OPS since the start of the 2025 season. The former World Series MVP will likely be looking for a deal in excess of $100 million next offseason as a free agent. If Crane and new general manager Randy Flores aren't prepared to make that commitment, now would be the time to maximize their return.

It would seem that either Peña or Isaac Paredes will be dealt this offseason. Paredes—who homered 25 times and drove in 94 runs in his second season with the Astros—will also be a free agent after the 2027 campaign.

It's fair to say that the Rangers seem more inclined to shed salary than add it this offseason.

In a perfect world, that would mean moving off an aging veteran. Two-time World Series MVP Corey Seager might draw trade interest, but he's still owed $157.5 million over the next five seasons and has an eight-team no-trade clause. Nathan Eovaldi ($24 million) and Jacob deGrom ($37 million) each have full no-trade clauses entering the final seasons of their contracts, with the latter already invoking his last summer to block a deal to the Braves .

MacKenzie Gore is a more realistic trade candidate than any of the trio mentioned. He doesn't have a full no-trade clause and is projected to make a more modest $8.7 million in his final year of arbitration eligibility. The 27-year-old lefty posted a 4.58 ERA in his first season with the Rangers, though both his 4.16 expected ERA and 3.87 FIP suggest he should have gotten better results.

Jerry Dipoto has been hesitant to trade from his starting rotation, but this offseason could be different for several reasons.

First, George Kirby's stock isn't as high as it was a few years ago. Between 2023 and 2024, he posted a 3.44 ERA across 64 starts. Over the last two seasons, he has had a much more modest 4.28 ERA. In his defense, Kirby does still have a 3.68 FIP over that period, so there may have been some bad luck.

Second, Kirby will pitch next season at 29 and has two arbitration seasons remaining. He's getting more expensive , with a projected 2027 salary of $9.8 million. Logan Gilbert can become a free agent after the 2027 season. You'd think the M's probably don't want to set up a scenario where they could lose Gilbert and Kirby in consecutive offseasons. They're not going to want to trade Kirby next winter when Gilbert is a free agent. (They could consider moving Gilbert this winter, theoretically, but he's their ace.)

Finally, the Mariners are in a position to withstand the loss of Kirby via trade this offseason. Gilbert is still under control for 2027, while Bryan Woo, Kade Anderson and Emerson Hancock would make for a pretty good rotation even without Kirby.

This offseason feels like a pivot point for the Athletics and Shea Langeliers. Either they reach a long-term extension with Langeliers—who homered 23 times and posted an .802 OPS in an All-Star campaign—or they trade him.

Technically, the A's don't have to make a decision on Langeliers this offseason, because he can't become a free agent until after the 2028 season. At this time next year, the A's will be getting ready to move into their permanent home in Las Vegas. They're not going to want to be subtracting then. It would be a much easier pill to swallow to trade Langeliers before their final season playing at a Triple-A ballpark.

Of course, the best-case scenario for the A's would be to work out a long-term deal with Langeliers. If the 29-year-old prefers to hit the open market after 2028, though, the new President of Baseball Operations Taylor Smith could offer him a bounty this winter.

We can't really be certain about anything with the Angels, who don't currently employ a manager and only have John Mozeliak running their front office through the end of December. Stan Kroenke's group may ultimately turn the Halos around, but Arte Moreno left a mess that will take multiple years to clean up.

The Angels might not be in a position to move Detmers until after the new CBA is in place, but the lefty will be a popular target if and when he's available. The 27-year-old southpaw finished sixth in AL Cy Young Award voting in 2026 and has two years of arbitration eligibility remaining.

Normally, there would be an argument for hanging onto Detmers and building around him. The Angels are so far away, though, that they would be wise to capitalize on a career year from Detmers, rather than holding onto him for a 2027 club that's almost certainly going to post the franchise's 12th consecutive losing campaign.

President of Baseball Operations Alex Anthopoulos has already squashed the idea of trading former NL MVP Ronald Acuña Jr., so let's move on to more likely outcomes.

The Braves were willing to float Spencer Strider last summer in trade talks with the Rangers for the aforementioned deGrom, per MLB.com's Mark Bowman . They'll likely be willing to listen again to the former All-Star righty.

The biggest question for the Braves is whether there's going to be real interest in Strider. Since finishing fourth in NL Cy Young Award voting in 2023, Strider has pitched to a 4.78 ERA over just 33 starts. The willingness to include Strider in the deGrom talks last summer, though, makes us think Anthopoulos could get creative again in trying to move off part or all of the $44 million he's owed over the next two seasons.

Brandon Marsh started in the All-Star Game at his home park this past summer, batting .301 with an .829 OPS in the first half. After the Midsummer Classic, Marsh was one of the worst players in baseball, hitting .184 with a .631 OPS.

Acquired from the Angels prior to the 2022 trade deadline, Marsh has been a very good Phillie. But he's a flawed player, one who hasn't developed into more than a strong-side platoon guy.

Prior to his contract year, he's an obvious trade candidate as the Phillies look to remake their outfield. Marsh could be dealt for an outfielder, or if the Phillies sign a replacement , he could be moved to address another area of need, such as a reliever.

Maybe we're being cynical, but the Marlins' entire existence suggests they'll seriously consider trade offers for Sandy Alcantara this offseason.

Alcantara is arguably the greatest pitcher in franchise history. He re-emerged as the most durable starter in the sport this past season, logging an MLB-high 214 innings. It was a no-brainer for the Fish to pick up the former NL Cy Young Award winner's $21 million club option for 2027.

Nonetheless, Alcantara is entering his contract year and probably won't be looking to sign a second consecutive team-friendly pact next winter. The Marlins could keep Alcantara now and dangle him if they aren't contending next summer, although carrying that injury risk might not make sense.

Spencer Nusbaum of The Athletic recently reported that the Nationals don't seem likely to trade CJ Abrams this offseason. We're not disputing that's the thinking right now, but plans can change.

Abrams is one of the best-hitting infielders in baseball, coming off a campaign that saw him hit 33 home runs and drive in 106 runs. Moving him to second base during the season was clunky, but it was probably the right move. He has a good enough bat to create immense value at any defensive position.

So why would the Nationals trade Abrams now? While they surprised with a 77-win season in 2026, their pitching—particularly in the bullpen—still isn't close to being ready to contend. Since winning the World Series in 2019, the Nationals haven't shown the willingness to spend the way they once did. It's possible that owner Mark Lerner is still waiting for the right offer to sell the club. Hanging over all of this is that Abrams is just two years away from free agency. He is on track to land a deal that nets him over $150 million. If the Nationals don't see themselves writing that check and don't think they are a playoff team in 2027, now could be the time to get the largest return for the two-time All-Star.

At least right now, letting Alonso walk in free agency last offseason looks to have been a disastrous decision by the President of Baseball Operations David Stearns.

While Alonso led the AL with 43 home runs and 113 RBI, the Mets got a .667 combined OPS at first base out of a group that included Mark Vientos, Jorge Polanco and Jared Young. They're stuck paying Polanco $20 million in 2027, but Vientos has likely run his course in Flushing. He's coming off a season where he batted .212 with a .652 OPS, and he doesn't have the same type of defensive flexibility as Brett Baty.

Vientos isn't that far removed from hitting 27 home runs for the Mets during the 2024 regular season, a campaign where he ultimately helped the club make an unlikely run to the NLCS. There's going to be interest in Vientos, who will turn 27 in December and has three years remaining before free agency. It's unlikely, though, that the Mets will get a significant return for him in a trade.

How sentimental will the Brewers get after winning their first World Series title?

Milwaukee seems pretty hell-bent on retaining reigning World Series MVP William Contreras, who is entering his contract year.

That makes us even more sure that they'll trade closer Trevor Megill before his walk year. Megill will forever be a legend in Milwaukee after closing out the first championship for the Brewers, but the 32-year-old is projected to make $8 million in his final year of arbitration. President of Baseball Operations Matt Arnold can trade Megill and get back a useful piece, while knowing that the trio of Abner Uribe, DL Hall and Aaron Ashby should still give manager Pat Murphy plenty of late-game options.

The book on Edward Cabrera during his five seasons in Miami was that he had frontline potential, but just couldn't stay healthy. Not only was he limited to 80 innings in his first season with the Cubs, but Cabrera also just wasn't effective, as evidenced by a 5.96 ERA.

With Matthew Boyd, David Peterson, Colin Rea, Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes all free agents, the Cubs could keep Cabrera for his penultimate year of arbitration eligibility and hope for a bounceback. Then again, with uncertainty also surrounding Justin Steele's health, the Cubs might be more inclined to move on from Cabrera and acquire someone more durable.

Presumably, the Pirates aren't ready to entertain trade offers for Paul Skenes or Oneil Cruz, although that day likely isn't far off unless Bob Nutting sells the team.

In the meantime, Carmen Mlodzinski could be someone Ben Cherington and company command interest in this offseason. As things stand right now, Mlodzinski would be on the outside looking in at a rotation that includes Skenes, Bubba Chandler, Jared Jones, Braxton Ashcraft and Mitch Keller. The Buccos could keep him as a swingman, but he may prove more valuable as a possible trade piece.

Mlodzinski has a 3.53 ERA in 146 MLB games over parts of four seasons, including 29 starts. A team needing starting-pitching depth might be able to help the Pirates plug another hole on their roster (second base?) if they're willing to take on Mlodzinski's three remaining arbitration years.

The initial inclination here was to put Alec Burleson, though Derrick Goold of The St. Louis Post-Dispatch recently reported that the Cardinals shut down trade inquiries into both him and shortstop Masyn Winn.

At catcher, the Cardinals have a surplus at a position that's coveted by other organizations. Even if we write Iván Herrera off as more of a DH, the Cardinals still have a slew of catchers. 22-year-old Leo Barnal is currently listed as their starter on Roster Resource , while Pedro Pagés and Jimmy Crooks saw significant time in 2026. The Cardinals could just option one of Pagés or Crooks, but that could create another logjam, as 19-year-old catcher Rainiel Rodriguez homered 23 times at Double-A last year and is already forcing his way towards the majors.

One or both of Pagés and Crooks will likely be traded this winter. Pagés will generate interest as a backup because he's posted 15 defensive runs saved and an eight fielding run value in parts of three MLB seasons.

The juiciest name possible here would be Elly De La Cruz, though with three years left until free agency, there should be no rush to part with the face of the franchise.

Spencer Steer is an interesting guy to watch because he is projected to make $5.7 million in his second-to-last year of arbitration eligibility. That's a decent chunk of change for the frugal Reds.

For a team looking to add right-handed hitting, Steer is coming off a campaign where he posted a 1.062 OPS against lefties. The soon-to-be 29-year-old also provides strong defensive flexibility, with experience at every position on the diamond except pitcher and catcher.

The Dodgers moved Teoscar Hernández from right to left field this past season. He responded by posting minus-six defensive runs saved and minus-six outs above average. At this stage of his career, it's clear he should be a DH and/or first baseman, neither of which the Dodgers can accommodate.

Hernández is due to make $17.34 million in the final guaranteed year of his contract. The Dodgers will likely have to pay down a portion of that, but Hernández has a track record of big hits and still hit .303 with a .907 OPS against lefties this past year. The 34-year-old will draw interest.

This one is pretty simple. With 20-year-old Ethan Salas taking over the reins as catcher, it's very unlikely that the Friars will retain both Freddy Fermin and Luis Campusano for next season.

Even though he's never graded out well behind the plate, Luis Campusano posted a .795 OPS this past season. He's probably a better fit to pair with Salas because he wouldn't be a dramatic offensive drop-off, plus he can take down some DH at-bats.

Fermin, 31, is projected to make $2.6 million in his first year of arbitration eligibility. His career 85 OPS+ might not stand out, but the 31-year-old has 45 career defensive runs saved behind the dish, which should intrigue teams.

Ketel Marte is the answer here because the team seemed exasperated with the former NLCS MVP during the 2026 season, which included him missing a game at Fenway Park on Aug. 17.

At the same time, Marte is owed $82 million over the next four seasons with an $11.5 million club option for 2031. Marte also gained a full no-trade clause via 10-and-5 rights during the 2026 season, so if he doesn't want to be traded, he can block any deal.

Marte still seems like the DBack most likely to be moved this offseason, but it's a pretty big blunder that Mike Hazen and company didn't trade him last winter before he gained the no-trade clause.

Casey Schmitt had a monster first half for the Giants in 2026, hitting 19 home runs and driving in 50 runs. After the All-Star Break, though, Schmitt hit just .189 with a .582 OPS in 10 games before a left meniscus tear ended his season.

The Giants should hardly let Schmitt burn a hole in their pockets, but they are much more likely to find a trade for him than for Jung Hoo Lee. With little roster flexibility, Buster Posey could move Schmitt for another area of need and/or a more established player. What about the Giants moving Schmitt in a deal with the Guardians that allows them to acquire Kwan? ESPN's Jeff Passan has also noted that the Giants have put Schmitt on the table when discussing trades for pitching help.

MLB Network's Jon Morosi recently reported that the Rockies could be more open to considering trade offers for Hunter Goodman than previously:

If Paul DePodesta is open for business, teams will be lined up to trade for Goodman. He's coming off of a 41-homer campaign for the Rockies and has three arbitration years remaining before free agency.

articles.title: New MLB Rumors on Yankees' Trade Talks After Maikel Garcia's Deal to Mariners From Royals
articles.summary: Before being traded from the Kansas City Royals to the Seattle Mariners on Wednesday, third baseman Maikel Garcia reportedly could have been headed to the East Coast.
articles.body:
Before being traded from the Kansas City Royals to the Seattle Mariners on Wednesday, third baseman Maikel Garcia reportedly could have been headed to the East Coast.

Jon Morosi of MLB.com reported that the New York Yankees "are involved in the 3B market," and they checked in with the Royals about Garcia before Wednesday's trade with the Mariners.

Garcia was sent to Seattle as part of a six-player trade that also acquired right-handed reliever James McArthur and minor league reliever LP Langevin in exchange for right-hander Bryce Miller, left-handed reliever Jose Ferrer and right-handed starter Logan Evans.

Known for his steady defense at the hot corner, Garcia was a first-time All-Star selection and Gold Glove Award winner in 2025, which helped him earn a five-year, $57.5 million contract last offseason. Unfortunately, he was limited to just 82 games in 2026 due to multiple stints on the injured list with hand and hamstring injuries. He hit .268 with three home runs and 68 RBI for a struggling Royals team that finished with a 69-93 record.

The Yankees have spent much of the offseason scouring for upgrades at third base over the incumbent Ryan McMahon, who hit just .213 with 11 home runs and 41 RBI in 124 regular-season games and .143 in the playoffs. Jon Heyman of the New York Post recently reported that the Yankees were "looking closely at" free-agent third baseman Alec Bohm, who had spent his entire seven-year career with the Philadelphia Phillies.

After losing out on Garcia, the Yankees will have to pivot elsewhere to fulfill their offseason goal of landing a quality third baseman.

articles.title: Xavier Taylor, 12-year old New Jersey Little Leaguer, dies 6 months after being hit by baseball
articles.summary: Taylor was placed in a coma after he suffered cardiac arrest.
articles.body:
Xavier Taylor, a 12-year-old Little League baseball player from New Jersey who was injured after being hit by a baseball in May, has died, his family announced.

Taylor was critically injured while warming up before a May 26 game when he was accidentally hit by a baseball in the neck. He was airlifted from Maple Shade, New Jersey, to Cooper University Hospital in Camden. The teenager was placed in a coma after suffering cardiac arrest.

"For the past five and a half months, the Nation has been lit up by the life of a remarkable 12-year-old boy from Maple Shade, New Jersey, Xavier Taylor," read a statement from the the Xavier Strong All Things Foundation said on social media "Xavier beat the odds of what doctors said would be impossible."

"For the past five and a half months, the Nation has been lit up by the life of a remarkable 12-year-old boy from Maple Shade, New Jersey, Xavier Taylor," read a statement from the the Xavier Strong All Things Foundation said on social media

"Xavier beat the odds of what doctors said would be impossible."

In a show of support as Taylor was hospitalized, the Philadelphia skyline and city landmarks, including the Ben Franklin Bridge, were lit up in blue during a June night . Local communities also showed their solidarity with the Little Leaguer by wearing his No. 6 jersey and placing baseball bats outside their homes. A meal train raised over $141,000 for the family.

The baseball world joined in with support as well. Philadelphia Phillies catcher Garrett Stubbs visited Taylor in June and gave him a signed bat; the Trenton Thunder of the MLB Draft League honored him before a game; and the Tampa Bay Rays sent the family a video .

"Thank you for being the light that you were on this earth. We will miss you, but your legacy will live on. We love you Xave," the foundation said.

articles.title: New Cubs Rumors on Teruaki Sato Pursuit, Jarren Duran Trade Interest amid Red Sox Buzz
articles.summary: The Chicago Cubs may be busy during this winter's free agency.
articles.body:
The Chicago Cubs may be busy during this winter's free agency.

According to Patrick Mooney of The Athletic, "league sources indicated the Cubs have extensively scouted Teruaki Sato, 27, the Japanese hitter whose left-handed power rates at or near the top of the scale. The club has also evaluated Boston Red Sox outfielder Jarren Duran as a potential change-of-scenery addition ahead of Friday's deadline to tender contracts to arbitration-eligible players, according to people familiar with the matter."

With Seiya Suzuki, Ian Happ and Carson Kelly potentially departing as free agents, the Cubs may need to restock their lineup. Quite a few teams are going to be in the hunt for Sato, however.

The Japanese star hit .306 with 39 homers, 106 RBI, 100 runs and a .991 OPS in 143 games for the Japan Central League's Hanshin Tigers this past season. After the immediate success of the Chicago White Sox's Munetaka Murakami this past season (35 homers, .825 OPS), the hope will be that Sato adjust equally as quickly at the MLB level.

While that isn't a guarantee, quite a few teams seem to have interest in his services:

There likely will be less of a market for the 30-year-old Durran, who hit .206 with 20 homers, 69 RBI, 66 runs and a .627 OPS in 2026. Trading for him would be a sign the Cubs are hoping he once again be the player who posted an .828 OPS in 2023 or an .834 OPS in 2024, but that's obviously not guaranteed.

But if Suzuki, Happ and Kelly depart this winter, the Cubs are going to have to focus on addressing the lineup. Sato would be a big splash; Durran would be more of a contingency plan.

articles.title: Lance Broadway, former top draft pick who ended career with Mets, dead at 43
articles.summary: The former MLB first-round pick died suddenly this week at 43 years old.
articles.body:
Lance Broadway, a first-round pick in the 2005 MLB draft and Hollywood actor , died suddenly this week at 43 years old.

The former pitcher passed away in an apartment complex stairwell on Tuesday in Texas, a rep for the Dallas County Medical Examiner confirmed to the California Post on Thursday.

A cause and manner of his passing are still pending testing, the rep said.

Broadway was born in Bryan, Texas, and after starring on the high school diamond, he joined Dallas Baptist University's baseball team and continued dominating, posting a minuscule ERA and two no-hitters in two seasons.

In 2005, he transferred to TCU, and after piling up 15 wins in 19 games, the Chicago White Sox selected him with the No. 15 overall pick in the MLB draft.

Broadway ended up making his Major League debut in September 2007, recording one strikeout in 2/3 of an inning pitched against the Minnesota Twins.

He remained with the White Sox until 2009, when he was traded to the Mets in a deal that included veteran catcher Ramón Castro.

Broadway only ended up appearing in eight more MLB games following the move to New York.

The Mets released Broadway after the season — and while he signed with the Blue Jays, did not make it past Triple-A.

In retirement, Broadway got into acting and garnered a role in the 2013 Gerard Butler flick "Olympus Has Fallen."

He also appeared in multiple TV series, including "Lucifer" and "Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D."

articles.title: Hyeseong Kim Set for Last Chance in Career-Defining 2027
articles.summary: Los Angeles Dodgers utility player Hyeseong Kim has to take a step up if he wants to remain with the team.
articles.body:
Los Angeles Dodgers utility player Hyeseong Kim is entering the final guaranteed year of his contract with the Dodgers, and has to take a step up if he wants to remain in Los Angeles.

Kim had a disappointing season in 2026 , appearing just 43 times in the first half of the season before the Dodgers banished him to Triple-A. Through a month and a half in MLB last season, Kim hit one homer and drove in 11 runs while posting a .651 OPS—noticeably worse than his .699 OPS from 2025.

After 2027, Kim has two years worth of club options, but he'll have to prove he deserves the $5 million per year he'd earn if the Dodgers pick up those options.

What Do the Dodgers Need to See From Hyeseong Kim?

Kim is and always has been a good baserunner and fielder , so it's obvious the Dodgers want him to improve with a bat—especially after his regression last season.

Dodgers Nation's Doug McKain thinks Kim has a huge opportunity to take a step forward after Miguel Rojas' retirement at the end of 2026.

"2027 is the most important year of Hyeseong Kim's MLB career," McKain said . "He's entering the final year of his guaranteed three-year, $12.5 million contract and the Dodgers really need to find out if the can be more than a defensive replacement and pinch runner. Because if he doesn't hit this year, he's gonna be gone.

"He's got a great opportunity with Miguel Rojas retiring. That opens the door for Hyeseong Kim. There's a need for infield depth. He could compete for playing time, but he has to prove that the bat belongs in the lineup. He's got the glove, he can run, he can defend, he can play multiple positions, but the Dodgers didn't bring him halfway around the world to be a permanent resident in Oklahoma City.

"At some point, potential has to turn into production."

The Dodgers are also clearly working through his offensive struggles, as general manager Brandon Gomes revealed the infielder is already taking steps to improve.

"We worked on some stuff at the end of the year that he felt pretty good about after presenting him plans, so I think he'll continue to work through those things and hopefully take a step forward on swing mechanics and getting him into a really good place offensively," Gomes said.

With these offensive improvements, Kim will look to finally get an extended run of games in MLB.

articles.title: Pete Rose Posthumously Pardoned by Trump After Baseball's Career Hits Leader Was Reinstated by MLB
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday said he had posthumously pardoned Pete Rose more than two years after the baseball star's death and a year after he was reinstated by Major League Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday said he had posthumously pardoned Pete Rose more than two years after the baseball star's death and a year after he was reinstated by Major League Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred .

"I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND," Trump posted on social media.

Rose, baseball's career hits leader at 4,256, entered guilty pleas on April 20, 1990, to two counts of filing false tax returns, admitting he failed to report $354,968 during a four-year period. That was about eight months after Rose agreed to a permanent ban from baseball.

″I know I'm not a bad person, but I did make some mistakes and it's in the eyes of the judge,″ Rose said that night during his weekly talk show on WCKY-AM in Cincinnati. ″All you can say is it's up to the judge.″

The pardon comes after Manfred issued a sweeping decision last May that opened a pathway for Rose to be considered for baseball's Hall of Fame. Manfred declared that individuals on MLB's permanently ineligible list would have their statuses restored at death, a ruling that impacted 17 people, most notably Rose and Shoeless Joe Jackson.

Under a rule adopted by the Hall's board of directors in 1991, anyone on the permanently ineligible list can't be considered for election to the Hall. The earliest Rose or Jackson could now be inducted would be in 2028.

Rose agreed to his permanent ban in August 1989 after Major League Baseball investigator John M. Dowd concluded he bet numerous times on the Cincinnati Reds while playing on and managing his hometown team from 1985-87.

Facing a sentence of up to six years in prison and $500,000 in fines, Rose was sentenced on July 19, 1990, by U.S. District Judge S. Arthur Spiegel in Cincinnati to five months in prison. He also was fined $50,000 and ordered to perform 1,000 hours of community service as a gym teacher's assistant with inner-city youths in Cincinnati as part of a one-year probation period. The first three months of the probation were to be spent at the halfway house.

Rose repaid the Internal Revenue Service $366,042.

"History and the tincture of time will decide his place among the all-time greats of baseball," Spiegel said. "With regard to Pete Rose, the individual, he has broken the law, admitted his guilt, and stands ready to pay the penalty. Under our system of law and sense of fairness, when he has completed his sentence, he will have paid his debt to society and should be accepted by society as rehabilitated. Only time will tell whether he is to be restored to his position of honor for his accomplishment on the ball fields of America."

Rose reported that Aug. 10 to the U.S. Penitentiary Marion Camp in Illinois, a minimum security facility, and was released Jan. 7, 1991. He entered Talbert House to start serving his probation and departed on April 5.

A 17-time All-Star during a playing career from 1963-86, Rose was the 1963 National League Rookie of the Year, 1973 MVP and 1975 World Series MVP. A three-time NL batting champion, he broke the prior hits record of 4,191 set by Ty Cobb from 1905-28.

AP Baseball Writer Jay Cohen contributed to this report.

articles.title: ‘I’m coming back’: Sonny Gray confirms Twins return after retirement talk following Red Sox exit
articles.summary: Sonny Gray is staying in Major League Baseball after agreeing to a two-year, $55 million deal with the Minnesota Twins.
articles.body: Sonny Gray is staying in Major League Baseball after agreeing to a two-year, $55 million deal with the Minnesota Twins. The 37-year-old right-hander is returning to a team he knows well after spending the 2026 season with the Boston Red Sox. Gray finished the year with 18 wins and a 2.72 ERA across 29 starts. His decision comes after he raised the possibility of retirement following Boston’s playoff exit. Now, he has another goal: helping Minnesota compete for a World Series title in 2027.Sonny Gray Confirms Minnesota Twins Return After Considering RetirementThe Twins confirmed Gray’s return on Wednesday, November 18. The pitcher also shared a message with Minnesota fans in a video posted by the team on X.“Hey Twins fans, this is Sonny Gray. I’m coming back. Can’t wait to see you at Target Field 2027.”It was a different message from the one Gray gave after Boston’s season ended. On September 30, he spoke about possibly leaving baseball to spend more time with his family. He had been taken out during the fifth inning of Game 2 against the New York Yankees in the American League Wild Card Series. At that point, he was unsure about his future.However, his thinking changed after speaking with his family. In an October 9 interview with The Boston Globe, Gray said returning for the 2027 season was an easy decision. He also made it clear that he still wanted to win a World Series.His latest season gives Minnesota plenty of reasons to feel good about the signing. Gray finished 2026 with an 18-5 record and a 2.72 ERA. He also recorded 149 strikeouts in 169 innings and finished fifth in American League Cy Young voting.The deal gives Gray a chance to continue his career while returning to a familiar place. He previously played for Minnesota in 2022 and 2023. During those two seasons, he recorded 16 wins and 13 losses with a 2.90 ERA across 56 starts. His 2023 season was particularly strong, as he earned an All-Star selection and finished second in AL Cy Young voting behind New York Yankees pitcher Gerrit Cole.According to ESPN's Jeff Passan, Gray's new contract is worth $55 million over two years and includes an option to leave after the first season. The agreement makes him the highest-paid pitcher in Twins history.Sonny Gray Gives Minnesota Twins More Rotation Options Alongside Joe Ryan and Pablo LópezGray's arrival also gives the Twins an important decision to make before the 2027 season. Minnesota already has several starting pitchers under contract, and adding another experienced arm makes the competition for rotation spots even tougher.Joe Ryan, Pablo López, Bailey Ober, Dean Kremer and Taj Bradley are among the pitchers who could feature in the starting rotation. Young pitchers such as Zebby Matthews, Mick Abel and Connor Prielipp also give the team more options.However, Pablo López's recovery will need attention. He missed the entire 2026 season after undergoing right elbow UCL surgery in February. His progress during spring training could affect how Minnesota plans its starting group.Taj Bradley is another name worth watching. The 25-year-old finished 2026 with a 12-6 record, a 3.73 ERA and 205 strikeouts across 178.1 innings. His improvement gives the Twins another reason to feel confident about their pitching options.Gray's arrival also comes with some concerns. His strikeout rate dropped to 21.8% in 2026, his lowest since 2016. His swinging-strike rate also fell to 9.9%. Still, his 2.72 ERA shows that he found ways to get results even without relying as much on strikeouts.Minnesota has also made a serious financial commitment this offseason. Catcher Ryan Jeffers accepted a $23.15 million qualifying offer for 2027 just one day before Gray's agreement. Together, the two deals represent more than $78 million in commitments.The Twins finished the 2026 season with a 77-85 record and missed the playoffs for another year. Bringing back Gray gives them an experienced starter who already knows the club and its home ground. articles.title: Trump posthumously pardons US baseball legend Pete Rose
articles.summary: Rose, who died in 2024, was given a lifetime ban from the sport for betting on games but was reinstated last year.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has posthumously pardoned baseball legend Pete Rose.

"I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday.

Rose, who died in 2024 at the age of 83, pleaded guilty in 1990 to two counts of filing false tax returns. He was also given a lifetime ban from Major League Baseball (MLB) after an investigation revealed he bet on games.

The baseball star was posthumously reinstated to MLB, in which he played for 24 seasons, last year and made eligible for the Baseball Hall of Fame.

Trump also said on Thursday that Rose's "record of 4,256 Hits in a Season will never be broken".

In fact, Rose accumulated a record 4,256 hits - which MLB defines as a batter striking the baseball into fair territory and reaching base without doing so via an error or a fielder's choice - during his career, which is more than any other player. He played a total of 3,562 games.

According to Trump, Rose "was treated terribly by Major League Baseball in not allowing him to go into the Baseball Hall of Fame. Politics, I guess".

The US Constitution gives a sitting president the broad power to grant a pardon, which represents legal forgiveness and ends any further punishment.

Because Rose's pardon was issued after his death, it is largely symbolic and does not change Rose's Hall of Fame status. The Department of Justice (DoJ) typically does not process posthumous pardon applications, though presidents have still issued them.

The BBC has contacted the Hall of Fame and the DoJ for comment.

The US president had previously floated the idea of pardoning Rose in March last year before the MLB reinstated him.

"Major League Baseball didn't have the courage or decency to put the late, great, Pete Rose, also known as 'Charlie Hustle,' into the Baseball Hall of fame," he wrote on Truth Social at the time.

"Now he is dead, will never experience the thrill of being selected, even though he was a FAR BETTER PLAYER than most of those who made it, and can only be named posthumously. WHAT A SHAME," Trump added.

MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred issued a decision in May 2025 that created a pathway for Rose to be eligible to be inducted into the baseball Hall of Fame - a ruling that also applied to 16 other people - as early as 2028.

In August 1989, Rose agreed to the permanent ban from the sport after MLB investigators found that he bet on his team, the Cincinnati Reds, multiple times while he was playing on and managing the team from 1985 to 1987.

In July 1990, after Rose admitted to failing to report $354,968 (£271,107) in income over a four-year period, he was sentenced to five months in prison. He also was fined $50,000 and ordered to perform community service at the time.
